changes.before: Change describe(4) to describe(std::string{"4"}). Which description is returned?
changes.after: Let input types choose a function and supply an omitted input with a default.

before: Functions may share a name when their parameter lists differ. An int argument can select an int overload while a string argument selects a string overload. These two example overloads do not use their input values, so their parameter names are omitted while their types remain declared.
Two functions cannot be distinguished merely by different return types with identical parameters. The call must have an unambiguous applicable signature.
A parameter such as int bonus = 1 uses that default when the argument is omitted. Passing zero explicitly is different from omitting the argument.
Avoid overlapping defaults that make a call ambiguous. In this example the bonus function has its own name, separate from the describe overloads.

Expected output or behavior: number
5. Local compiler test evidence is recorded separately from app reading completion.

Optional local transfer task: Call both describe overloads, then compare add_bonus(4) with add_bonus(4, 0). Explain both independent selection rules. You may trace this without a compiler; finishing the reading is not proof of a local run.
after: Overloads are functions with the same name but different parameter lists. Here one describe accepts an int and another accepts a string. Their inputs need no names because these bodies do not read their values.
The compiler uses the call's input types to choose an overload. A different return type alone cannot distinguish two functions with identical parameter lists.
A default argument supplies an input when the caller leaves it out. In add_bonus, bonus = 1 makes the bonus one when the call gives only a score.
The compiler needs one clear choice. If several overloads fit equally well, the call is ambiguous, meaning the compiler cannot choose. Defaults can cause this if too many functions fit the same call.
The program prints number, then 5 on the next line. describe receives an int. add_bonus receives four and uses its default bonus of one.
A default is used only when that argument is missing. If the caller supplies a bonus, that value is used even when it is zero.

before.question: Change describe(4) to describe(std::string{"4"}). Which description is returned?
choices: number because the characters look numeric.
text because the argument is a std::string.
before.explanation: Overload selection uses argument types, not the appearance of the stored characters.

after.question: Change describe(4) to describe(std::string{"4"}). Which description is returned?
choices: number, because the text looks like a number.
text, because the argument is a std::string.
after.explanation: The argument's type selects the string overload. Its characters do not change its type.
